title: The four senses of scripture (CCC 115–119)
hookLine: literal, allegorical, moral and anagogical: one text, many depths

cards: On a piano stand, a sheet of music lies open. A beginner reads the notes, one at a time, and gets them right. A teacher, reading the same page, hears the harmony moving underneath.
The composer sees where the whole piece is heading, pages ahead. Nobody has changed a single note; the depth of the reading changed.
The Catholic tradition reads scripture a little like that: the same verse, read on several levels at once. Today's word: the four senses.

teach.b: The Catechism names two senses of scripture, the literal and the spiritual, then divides the spiritual into three.
Four in all: literal, allegorical, moral, anagogical. Underneath everything, the literal: what the words actually say, what the writer meant.
Following Thomas Aquinas, the Catechism says every other sense is built on this one. Then the allegorical: how events point to Christ. Paul uses the very word.
Writing about Abraham's two sons in Galatians, he says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Which things are said by an allegory." Then the moral: what the text asks of how we live.
Paul again, about Israel in the desert: these things "are written for our correction." Then the anagogical: where it all leads in the end, toward the life of heaven.
The Catechism's own example of the allegorical sense is the crossing of the Red Sea, a sign of Christ's victory and of Christian baptism.
Some readers run that story through all four. Literally, Israel walks through the sea and out of slavery. Allegorically, Christ's victory, and baptism.
Morally, leaving behind what holds a person captive. Anagogically, the last crossing, into the promised land.

The Catechism also quotes a medieval rhyme that packs it into a pocket: the letter teaches what happened; allegory, what to believe; the moral sense, what to do; anagogy, where you're heading. It isn't a secret code.
The literal comes first, and the other senses grow out of it, not away from it. The page stays the same. The reading goes deeper.

how: Catholic preachers and readers draw on the four senses when they explain scripture, and the Church's liturgy often pairs an Old Testament story with a Gospel reading so that one sheds light on the other.

games.q: Israel walks through the sea and out of Egypt. the Catechism gives an allegorical reading of it. which one?
o: a lesson in courage under pressure
a sign of Christ's victory and of baptism
games.why: the Catechism's allegorical example is the Red Sea crossing as a sign of Christ's victory and of Christian baptism. courage would be a moral reading; heaven, an anagogical one.

practice: Say this line from the Psalms slowly, in the Douay-Rheims: "I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord."

Then ask four questions, a breath between each: what happened, pilgrims setting off for the temple in Jerusalem; what might it show about Christ; what does it ask of me today; and where is it heading, in the end?
Some may stay unanswered, and that's fine; if you pray, say the line again as your own.

wordCard.voice: Four senses. Literal, allegorical, moral and anagogical: one text read at four depths, with the literal underneath them all. Today's word.
